October 28th, 2026

CVE ID

AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H
Affected Vendors
Valkey
Affected Products
Valkey
Vulnerability Details
This vulnerability allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Valkey. Authentication is required to exploit this vulnerability.
The specific flaw exists within the handling of the parameters supplied to the PUBLISH message handler. The issue results from the lack of proper validation of user-supplied data, which can result in an incorrect calculation before allocating a buffer. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the service account.
Additional Details
Valkey has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at:

items.content:
Download
v1
https://www.unknowncheats.me/forum/d...=file&id=58964
This is a runtime version of my IL2CPP dumper. Instead of reading the metadata straight from disk, it runs inside the game and dumps the metadata that's already loaded in memory.
I mainly made it for games where global-metadata.dat is encrypted, packed or otherwise protected. That includes common packers/protectors like Themida, and similar setups where the on-disk metadata is scrambled, encrypted, or not readable as a normal global-metadata.dat. Offline dumpers fail there because they try to parse the protected file. This one reads from the live process instead. Depending on how the game handles its metadata, IL2CPP may have already unpacked or decrypted what it needs into memory, so the dump can come from the runtime data rather than the protected disk copy.
It won't work with games protected by anti-cheats like EAC, so don't try injecting it into those.
Features
- Dumps loaded assemblies, classes, fields and methods
- Includes parent classes, interfaces, nested types and enums
- Generates C++, C#, Rust, Python and JSON output
- Includes an index and per-assembly C# files
- Exports field offsets and method RVAs using names like _Offset and _RVA
- Dumps metadata from memory to handle certain encrypted or packed metadata setups
- Tries to handle renamed modules and stripped/missing IL2CPP exports
Output
The dump is saved to Desktop\GameDump, with C:\GameDump used as a fallback.
Files include:
- GameDump.hpp
- GameDump.cs
- GameDump.rs
- GameDump.py
- GameDump.json
- Index.json
- images\ containing per-assembly .cs files
How to use
1. Start the game and wait for IL2CPP to initialise. The main menu is usually enough.
2. Inject dumper.dll into the process.
3. A console titled IL2CPP Dumper should open and show the progress.
4. Once it finishes, check the output folder.
The dumper also tries to detect renamed modules, such as UserAssembly.dll, if the game doesn't use GameAssembly.dll. There's also a fallback scan for when the usual exports aren't available.
Notes
- x64 only
- This release contains the runtime DLL only.
- If the metadata is unprotected and readable on disk, a normal offline dumper is probably the easier option.
- Intended for protected metadata setups; compatibility depends on how the game handles its metadata.
If you run into any issues or find a game it doesn't handle properly, post the details here.

现代实验产生的数据量，远远超出了科学家能够深入研究的范围。如今，研究人员可以改变数千个基因，并测量这些改变对数百万个细胞的影响。但要理解这些结果对人类疾病意味着什么，就需要将复杂的实验发现与几十年来分散积累的科学知识联系起来。在这方面，AI 可以帮助科学家发掘原本可能被忽略的有潜力的线索。
“我们构建细胞图谱，是为了让其他科学家能够做出我们尚未想到的发现。AI 可以帮助更多研究人员探索这些资源，把意料之外的观察结果转化为有待验证的新问题。”
—Sarah Teichmann，Ph.D.，University of Cambridge 干细胞医学讲席教授、Human Cell Atlas 创始联席主席
团队将分析任务分配给数千个由 GPT‑Rosalind 驱动的 AI 智能体，我们将这种方法称为分布式生物学推理。这些智能体研究了一个
全脑 CRISPR 图谱
⁠
（在新窗口中打开）
，该数据集展示了基因破坏如何影响小鼠全脑中不同类型的细胞。每个智能体负责研究一种基因破坏，分析细胞反应、检索科学文献，并对结果提出解释。它们的报告被汇总成一份推理图谱，将基因、细胞层面的影响、相关文献以及可能的生物学机制联系起来。
研究团队估计，如果由人类逐一分析每种扰动，完成同等程度的分析和文献回顾将需要数月到一年。智能体复现了人工分析的发现，同时找到了更多线索。它们对新颖性和科学价值的评估，也与盲评中人类专家的判断一致。这些发现有助于确定后续实验的优先顺序，以验证所提出的生物学机制。
其中一些见解为理解脑部疾病提供了新线索。智能体发现，两个与疾病相关的基因对脑细胞的影响存在意料之外的差异，同时还发现了胆固醇调控与神经退行性病变之间的潜在关联。这些发现可以帮助科学家研究疾病如何发生发展，以及未来的治疗可能从何处干预。
“有时线索早已存在，散落在不同领域——只是我们还没有把它们联系起来。神经元功能与胆固醇代谢之间可能存在的联系表明，一旦把这些零散的信息拼在一起，就能为我们理解疾病的生物学机制提供新的思路。”
—Tomasz Nowakowski，Ph.D.，UCSF 神经外科副教授
研究人员现在就可以开始探索这些发现。这份推理图谱
已公开
⁠
（在新窗口中打开）
，科学家可以借此比较相关基因、研究意料之外的反应，并找到值得深入探索的有潜力的线索。当不同领域的研究人员汇聚各自的专业知识，以出人意料的方式将熟悉的概念联系起来时，往往就会产生新发现。AI 可以将新数据与分散在各学科中的知识关联起来，大幅拓展这种跨领域联系的规模。这带来的机遇不仅仅是加快数据分析。将 AI 与实验生物学、人类专业知识及科学文献相结合，我们可以帮助科学家把更多数据转化为可验证的设想。
大规模实验中的意外线索
实验中一些最有意思的线索，往往不在科学家最初打算研究的范围内。在涵盖数千种扰动的数据集中，这些线索很容易被忽略。
智能体发现了 Tsc1 和 Tsc2 之间一项意料之外的差异。这两个基因共同调控 mTOR，而 mTOR 是细胞生长、代谢和衰老的重要调节因子。在多个神经元群体中，破坏其中任一基因产生的影响都相似。但在帮助协调运动的小脑中，破坏 Tsc2 改变了数十个参与神经元通信的基因的活性，而破坏 Tsc1 几乎没有引起变化。
这一差异可能与人类疾病有关。在结节性硬化症患者中，小脑异常与 TSC2 突变密切相关。虽然降低 mTOR 活性的药物可以治疗某些脑肿瘤和癫痫发作，但与该疾病相关的学习和行为障碍仍然难以解决。智能体锁定了一群特定的神经元及值得研究的细胞变化：哪些变化可能通过现有药物得到纠正，哪些又可能指向新的治疗方法？这为研究人员提供了一组更具体的问题，可在实验室中进行验证。
分工协作，深化推理
让单个智能体处理整个数据集，能否达到数千个智能体并行工作的效果？我们在模型和资源保持不变的条件下对此进行了测试。随着工作量增加，单个智能体检索的文献越来越少：在工作量最大时，它仅引用了 11 篇文献，而分布式智能体引用了 700 多篇。人类专家也更认可分布式智能体给出的解读。
科学家的时间有限，往往会重点关注数据中最显著的信号。分布式智能体能够帮助考察更广泛的反应，包括细微或意料之外的反应，并将其与相关科学文献联系起来。并行运行智能体，可以同时研究多种扰动。这有助于科学家更充分地挖掘实验中的信息，发现原本可能被忽略的有潜力的线索。

找到下一个值得开展的实验
当一项发现能指向值得开展的实验时，它就更有价值。智能体在
DCTN1
基因中发现了这样一条线索。该基因的突变会导致 Perry 综合征，这是一种具有帕金森病样症状的神经退行性疾病。
DCTN1 参与神经元内部的物质运输。在全脑 CRISPR 图谱中，破坏 Dctn1 会提高参与胆固醇合成的基因的表达水平。智能体将这一观察结果与已有研究联系起来；这些研究提示，胆固醇运输出现问题可能会导致细胞合成更多胆固醇。这为后续实验提出了一个问题：破坏 DCTN1 是否会改变胆固醇在神经元内的分布？这些变化是否会促成神经退行性病变？如果是，恢复胆固醇的正常分布是否有助于保护神经元？
人类专家也认为，这一假设新颖、意义重大，值得进一步研究。这个例子表明，将意料之外的结果与现有知识联系起来，可以把一条线索转化为可验证的设想，甚至为疾病治疗开辟新方向。
在盲评比较中，75% 的情况下，人类专家更认可分布式智能体的报告，而非单个智能体的报告。
科学家始终是科学发现的核心。通过发掘更多有潜力的线索，AI 可以帮助研究人员决定哪些设想值得深入探索、设计实验并解读结果。我们的目标是将生物学实验中的更多信息转化为知识，逐步为研发更好的药物提供指导。

items.text: bhis-blog published: John Strand's 11 Core Skills: For SOC Analysts
items.title: John Strand's 11 Core Skills: For SOC Analysts
items.content:
The cybersecurity battlefield evolves daily, with SOC analysts serving as front-line defenders. After years of training SOC teams, I’ve identified 11 core skills that separate effective defenders from the rest.
Here’s the problem: we’re training analysts to look for needles in haystacks when they don’t even know what hay looks like. Too many enter SOC positions without understanding the systems they’re trying to protect.
1. Understanding Operating Systems
You can’t defend what you don’t understand. Period. Master both Windows and Linux. Not just surface stuff, but really get how they work under the hood. Learn through the incident response lens:”If this system were hacked, how would I find the bad guys?”
2. Network Traffic Analysis
Understand TCP/IP and how traffic actually flows (the OSI model matters less than knowing what a SYN flood, DNS tunnel, or C2 beacon looks like on the wire). Know the difference between TCP and UDP, and establish baselines for what normal traffic looks like in your environment.
3. Memory Analysis
Memory forensics shows you malware that might be invisible on disk. Tools like Volatility let you examine processes, connections, and DLLs from a memory dump. This works even when attackers delete their tools or use fileless malware. It’s like catching someone with their hand in the cookie jar.
4. Log Analysis
Logs are your investigative breadcrumbs. Know which ones to collect and how to make sense of them. Remember, no single log tells the whole story. You need to connect multiple data points, like a detective piecing together clues at a crime scene.
5. Endpoint Detection and Response
Master your EDR solutions. Understand how they work, what they can do, and where they fall short. No EDR catches everything. You need to tune these tools, like adjusting the sights on a rifle for better accuracy.
6. Threat Hunting
Don’t just sit back waiting for alerts. Get out there and hunt! Look for threats that slipped past your automated systems. Combine smart hypotheses with data analysis to find attackers living off the land, using legitimate tools for evil purposes.
7. Malware Analysis
Every SOC analyst should know basic static and dynamic analysis. Look at the file without running it, then observe its behavior in a safe sandbox. Learn to spot common techniques like obfuscation and persistence. Know thy enemy, right?
8. Vulnerability Management
Understand different vulnerability types and how they’re exploited. Don’t just focus on CVSS scores. Consider actual exploitability in your environment and the potential impact. A “critical” vulnerability that can’t actually be exploited in your environment isn’t critical for you.
9. Incident Response
When stuff hits the fan, know what to do. Identify what happened, contain it, kick out the attackers, and recover your systems. Document everything. Not just for compliance, but so your team can learn and improve.
10. Automation and Scripting
Automate the boring stuff with PowerShell, Python, or Bash. Create tools that do the repetitive work for you. This frees you up to focus on the complex problems that need human brainpower.
11. Communication and Documentation
Technical skills alone won’t cut it. You need to explain complex technical stuff to different audiences. The most brilliant analysis in the world is useless if you can’t make the bosses understand why they should care.
Conclusion
Mastering these skills won’t happen overnight, but they’re the foundation of being an effective SOC analyst. What makes great analysts stand out isn’t just knowing individual skills but connecting dots across domains: seeing how network traffic ties to endpoint behavior, when log weirdness might point to memory-resident malware, and how vulnerabilities create openings for attackers
By building these core skills, you’ll be ready to protect your organization against even the nastiest threats out there..

items.text: cisco-advisory published: Cisco Secure Firewall Adaptive Security Appliance and Secure Firewall Threat Defense Software Remote Access SSL VPN Tunnel Denial of Service Vulnerability
items.title: Cisco Secure Firewall Adaptive Security Appliance and Secure Firewall Threat Defense Software Remote Access SSL VPN Tunnel Denial of Service Vulnerability
items.content:
A vulnerability in the Remote Access SSL VPN service of Cisco Secure Firewall Adaptive Security Appliance (ASA) Software and Cisco Secure Firewall Threat Defense (FTD) Software could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to cause the device to reload unexpectedly, resulting in a denial of service (DoS) condition. This vulnerability is due to logic errors when secondary authentication is configured on a tunnel group. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a crafted request when connecting to the SSL remote access VPN. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to cause the affected device to reload, resulting in a DoS condition. Cisco has released software updates that address this vulnerability. There are no workarounds that address this vulnerability. This advisory is available at the following link: https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-asaftd-tunnel-dos-s6mgkb75
Security Impact Rating: High

items.content: 过去两年，LLM 应用基本不用操心对话状态放在哪；Responses API 和实时语音把状态推向服务端之后，这个问题落到了推理引擎上。SGLang 把交互规则固定成上层接口，把引擎的基本单位从单次请求改成持续会话。这条路在哪种架构上站得住、代价是什么、和 vLLM-Omni、LiveKit、Pipecat 的答案有何不同。

It's already been over two weeks since my last recap, so it's time to catch up on what's been happening lately.
Nyatabi Hits the App Store
Last time, I mentioned running into so many headaches after a trip that I decided to build an app. At the end of my last post, I wrote, "Musubicho is still in development and not finished yet." Less than two weeks later, I renamed it Nyatabi (喵旅) and officially launched it on the App Store. That said, I haven't even been the first one to really test it out in the wild. I'm such a homebody that even though a trip sparked the project, I haven't had the chance to use all its features myself yet. I just love building products—created purely out of passion.
It's live on the App Store now, and I put together a decent landing page for it. Feel free to check it out! (Though it's iOS-only for now.)
Nyatabi — your AI travel companion for iPhone
Plan with Musubi, explore together, split spending fairly and turn your route into memories. Your whole journey, in one local-first iPhone app.
Nyatabi
Beyond helping you map out trips, it lets an agent handle expense tracking and bill splitting on the go (either by snapping receipts or just telling it what you spent). In group chats, the agent can scout nearby restaurants or pull up your friends' locations. And once the trip wraps up, you can replay your route, generate an auto-edited highlight video, or export a detailed travel footprint report.
Before the official release, I shot a 4-part short video series walking through the entire flow: pre-trip planning → snapping receipts to split expenses on the go → settling balances with minimum transfers → everyday roommate bookkeeping. On October 16, I posted a full 2-minute demo.
Along the way, I also open-sourced the rounded-line icon set used in Nyatabi at
icons.nyatabi.app
.
Engineering shortcuts vs. engineering rigor: refusing to be a human test runner, I wired up XCUITest across two physical iPhones so agents could handle the entire closed loop of "implement → verify → fail → fix" on their own (check out my technical post, "
My AI-Native iOS Development & Verification Workflow
", for details).
It could be handy whether you're traveling or just going about everyday life: I've always found life-logging footprint apps a bit awkward to use, so I baked my own footprint features right in to track daily routines as well. I don't want to turn this into a full-on product pitch, so I'll stop here. If you're interested, feel free to give it a spin.

AI in the Trenches
A Love-Hate Relationship with Claude
I had a backup Claude alt account that managed to hold out for over two weeks, so I decided to upgrade it. Went from Pro to Max, only to get slapped with an instant ban—no refund, either. I was so anxious that night that I stayed up by myself until 5 a.m. Eventually, I couldn't help setting up yet another account, and that one's somehow still alive.
On top of that, my $DRAM shares kept tumbling before I could break even, so those days felt like a brutal double blow from Anthropic and $DRAM. It also got me calculating the real cost of compute inflation: last year, a $20 Claude subscription felt like it could do so much; now, even the $200 Max tier barely scratches the surface. By comparison, Apple's $99/year developer membership is so cheap it's almost moving.
OpenAI's "God Tier" Account and Kimi Falling Flat on Its Face
There was a funny little detour along the way. Around the 20th, I noticed a bug in OpenAI: an old 20x subscription was still usable even after downgrading or canceling. I honestly thought I'd struck gold with some chosen "god-tier" account. But by day five of freeloading, the bug got patched and my quota went straight to zero.
Then on the 23rd, I dropped $19 on Kimi, wanting to see how it compared to $20 Claude. I asked it to write a website footer—and before it even finished, barely ten minutes in, I slammed right into a 5-hour rate limit. Might as well just call yourselves QueueShot AI. When it comes to domestic models, everyone should just use DeepSeek—what are the rest of these garbage knockoffs even doing? DeepSeek is the only one that can actually play: no token sales, no bullshit. The API pricing is right there: take it or leave it. The TPS is right there too—DeepSeek 4.1 Flash pushes over 200 TPS, and at those prices, burn through as much as you want.
Unlike Kimi—their greed this time is honestly shameless: zero compute power, but pulling that classic Lei Jun artificial scarcity playbook and taking users for fools to the extreme.
Ryugi (流儀) — Open-Source Claude Artifacts
After getting jerked around like that, I thought: why not just build my own version of Claude Artifacts? I genuinely love using that feature. For docs, artboard designs, and architecture sketches, it's just so damn good—a product genuinely made with care.
But being locked into Claude's proprietary subscription was a dealbreaker. So what choice did I have? Build it myself.
Claude Artifacts support five types, and the ones I use most are Artboard, Document, and HTML. Sick of taking Anthropic's nonsense, I cobbled together a standalone workbench called "Ryugi" (
ryugi.innei.dev
).
Building this brought an unexpected bonus too: it completely changed my view of Codex's design skills. I used to think Codex was garbage at design, and just on the 10th I had tweeted about how miserable it was trying to write UI with it. But once I plugged it into Ryugi's Artboard workflow, it turned out to be surprisingly solid—I guess I was just using it wrong before. To my surprise, that tweet blew up, racking up 93K impressions and over 700 bookmarks.
I've been using it for a few days now, putting it through heavy daily use and constantly refining it. The cloud environment is live too, so now it helps me brainstorm, work on designs, hash out architecture docs, and even knock out small feature requests on the side.
The experience genuinely captures the vibe of Claude Artifacts now. Hooking this workflow up to other harnesses—like DeepSeek or Codex—makes them dramatically more useful. If you haven't tried it yet, you really should.

LobeHub Bids Farewell to AntD
On the work front: I've been here for almost a year now. Back when I first joined, I declared that I was going to ditch AntD once and for all. That turned into a ten-month marathon, but on the 9th of this month, I finally pulled it off—migrating everything over to
@base_ui
+
StyleX
(meaning
lobe-ui
v6).
Looking back at the numbers, the engineering scale was pretty wild:
lobe-ui
rewrote 54 components on top of Base UI, and AntD dependencies in
lobe-editor
,
lobe-charts
, and
lobe-icons
were completely eliminated.
The main repo has over 11,000 TypeScript files. Replacing the underlying component library spanned 28 PRs and touched 3,242 files, with the single largest PR modifying 1,040 files.
Along the way, we also migrated our CSS-in-JS setup to StyleX, slashing the original 179 emotion files down to just 3. The most satisfying part was running 5 agents across parallel branches: in three and a half hours, they plowed through 84 commits. We then ran regression tests across 45 routes using 1,000 screenshot comparisons and computed-style diffs, reliably catching 4 regressions.
Getting rid of AntD paid off right away. Bundle sizes shrank dramatically, and pages feel noticeably snappier. Thinking back, before AI agents existed, a core refactor of this scale would have easily taken an entire team a full quarter of grinding. But with today's models being so capable, I managed to knock out this massive project almost entirely on my own.
The Story Ends Here
Throughout October, blind dates from family and friends were nonstop, but most of the time chatting was pretty draining. Earlier in the month, I tweeted a rant saying some WeChat chats feel like "an LLM running on a potato server, taking hours of inference just to spit out a few characters, and if you don't send a request, you'll never get a response." That tweet unexpectedly racked up over 70,000 views, and predictably enough, I got hit with the "you're a nice guy" card in real life soon after.
But just a few days later, through another blind date, I unexpectedly met someone I could genuinely click with—something that hadn't happened in a long time.
I find myself wanting deeper conversations lately—talking about fundamental values, life outlooks, and thoughts on the future. In day-to-day life, finding someone who can actually match that energy is rare. But that night—which also happened to be our last conversation—we talked about so much. Beyond having plenty of shared interests, what hit hardest was a real resonance in who we are deep down. Just knowing someone on that exact same wavelength actually exists was a wonderful, lucky surprise.
Unfortunately, she felt our personalities were just too similar to be a good match. In the end, we parted ways gracefully, and that was where the story ended.
Turning My Resume into a Canvas
Another project I spent a lot of time on was completely rebuilding my personal resume page for Programmer's Day on October 24, launching it at
resume.innei.in/lab/
.
The spark was simple: surfing online recently, I saw a few personal sites and resumes that looked amazing, so I wanted to bring my own ideas into the mix and polish up something of my own. A traditional single-page format can't hold very much, so I turned it into a canvas you can freely pan, zoom, and explore—connecting all the projects I've worked on and milestones I've reached over the six or seven years since college into one continuous timeline.
Working on this canvas also ended up unlocking some new skills. To give the page some fitting background music, I dove into arranging with realistic virtual instruments, tweaking synthesis, and fine-tuning the details (huge thanks to
@wibus_wee
for walking me through Ozone mastering), and I even built an interactive sheet music display into the canvas.
Cramming a bunch of music arrangement and audio mastering just to build a resume was an unexpected bonus. Once I get around to picking music theory back up properly, I really should build an app for instruments and music theory.
